newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany lifts jobless forecast as tax income drops.
newsitem.headline: Germany lifts jobless forecast as tax income drops.

text.p: Germany said on Sunday it was raising its unemployment forecast for 1997, an increase that tears a hole in the government's budget and hurts the country's chances of qualifying for the single European currency.
A spokesman for the Finance Ministry said the government had lifted its forecast for average unemployment this year by about 120,000 from an earlier prediction of 4.1 million.

He said the government had made a number of other revisions, which he declined to detail. But he said Germany was sticking with its estimate that gross domestic product (GDP) would rise by 2.5 percent this year.

"We have raised the unemployment forecast for the full year because of the current job market conditions," the spokesman said. But he declined to comment on reports that first quarter tax revenues would be far below expectations.
The government is to receive a report later this week detailing first quarter tax revenues.
The eagerly awaited report due on Thursday will be put together by the government, its council of economic advisers, independent economic research institutes, municipalities, and the Bundesbank.
The Sunday newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported that tax shortfalls to be announced in the report will blow a 20-billion mark hole in Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 budget.
"It doesn't make any sense to speculate about these figures beforehand," the finance ministry spokesman said.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) have been saying that the 1997 deficit would be 20 billion marks larger than Waigel expects because of falling tax revenues and the higher unemployment.
Waigel said in late April that the shortfall could be 10 billion marks but would "definitely not" be as high as the SPD estimate of 20 billion marks.

The conservative Welt am Sonntag newspaper quoted finance ministry sources as saying the massive unemployment and the weak consumer demand from private households were responsible for the gloomy outlook on the budget.
"It could be 20 billion marks plus who knows how much," the newspaper quoted the finance ministry source saying.
Kohl, who has been counting on a decline in unemployment from its post-war high this year, admitted last week that he saw no turnaround in the rising jobless trend this year.
"This year will not bring a change in the trend for the labour market, especially not as high as I would wish," Kohl said. But halving unemployment by 2000 was still his goal.
"It is our goal. I cannot say whether it will be reached."

Unemployment fell by 130,000 in April from March to 4.347 million, a rate of 11.3 percent, but was still 480,000 higher than a year earlier. Stripping out seasonal factors, dole queues lengthened by 8,000 to 4.299 million.
Containing unemployment is a key factor in Germany's bid to cut state borrowing this year to qualify for European monetary union, which is scheduled to start in 1999.
Government projections, which foresee cutting the fiscal deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of gross domestic product, assume average joblessness of 4.1 million in 1997.
But unemployment far above that level so far this year has already blown the jobless benefits budget of Germany's Federal Labour Office for the entire year.
